name: work-decide
description: 'Takes the owner through the decisions his work items wait on, each with a recommendation, and records his answers. Use when he asks "what do you need from me", answers a waiting decision ("go with option B"), or states a project-wide decision. Not for a bare "yes" when this chat asked no question.'

# Work decide

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. Build the queue: requirements waiting for approval, designs marked proposed, items at stage 11 waiting for result approval, Open Questions rows where the owner decides, and memory proposals (records saved as `needs-review` because the owner did not answer "Save to memory?"). The command lists each decision once. Its "Agent to-do" lines are the agent's own steps, not decisions waiting on the owner: count and show only the decisions. A delivery offer, as an agent to-do or as an open question, belongs to `work-delegate`, the only skill that makes or records it: open it after the owner's other decisions.
   `toolkit work decisions`
2. The owner gave an answer without being asked ("approved", "go with B"): match it to exactly one waiting decision. If two could match, ask which one, naming both. A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" is not such an answer ("What counts as an answer").
3. Otherwise take the decisions one at a time, the one blocking the most work first. For each: what is being decided, the choices, your recommendation and its main reason, and what happens after each answer. Every decision carries a recommendation, even when it is the only one in the queue; a bare question is not enough. One decision per message, asked in the reply text.
4. A requirements approval: save his words as a history note first, so no later session asks him again. Then check the Agreed goal and the open questions. The goal still holds the template text: write the goal he was shown with the approval question, then record the approval. A requirement still has an open question linked: say which one, open `work-requirements` for it, and record the approval, without asking him again, once it is answered.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner'\''s words: <quote>' --effect 'Requirements approval to record.'`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --text '<goal he was shown>'`
5. Record each answer where it belongs. Approvals (for requirements, first set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and put who approved it and when in its Decision record, as `work-requirements` step 8 does; after it, a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design` unless the owner agreed to skip the design, and a skip is said in the final reply). The approve command marks the Open Questions rows that asked for that approval Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; read that line, and do not mark those rows again by hand. An Open Questions answer: rewrite that row with the answer, the date, and status Answered (the delivery offer row: open `work-delegate`, which records it).
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --result --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --set-file <file>`
   Then, for an approval or an answer: `waiting_on` set to `agent` when the agent continues (the approve command sets it to `none` by itself), unless another question for him on that item is still open; then one history note in the owner's words, with an `--effect` that says what the answer changes (a requirements approval has its note from step 4).
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner'\''s words: <quote>' --effect '<what the answer changes>'`
6. A memory proposal: show its one line and whether you recommend keeping it. The agent does not rely on it until he approves it. Yes: approve it, and it becomes a current memory. No: reject it (the proposal is deleted), and never propose the same fact again under other words.
   `toolkit memory approve <key> --by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory reject <key>`
7. A decision for the whole project: add a `DECISIONS.md` row and save it with `publish-docs`. Run the command inside the worktree `publish-docs` opens, then let it commit (and push, when the project has a remote).
   `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner>`
8. A "no" or a change: record it as the answer, move the item back (for example to refinement), and open the skill that redoes the work.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
9. Lead with "Not saved" if any write failed. When an answer changed an item's next step, update the current focus (`../../references/conventions.md`, "The current focus"). When the queue is empty, say so and offer to continue unblocked items with `work-on`. End the reply with the next decision's question, or the exact words that continue.

## What counts as an answer

- Only the owner's explicit words count. Quote them in the history note. The lifecycle command prints the full approval rules:
  `toolkit work lifecycle`
- A question, a suggestion, a tentative answer ("probably B"), or silence is not an answer. Ask again in one line.
- An approval covers only what was shown. It never covers merge, deployment, spending, or publishing.
- A bare "yes", "ok", or "looks good" answers only a question asked earlier in this conversation. When none was asked, or the waiting question is not a yes-or-no question, show the decision with its choices and your recommendation, and record nothing.
- Set `waiting_on` to `agent` when the agent can continue, to `none` when nothing waits, or keep `owner` when another owner question is still open on that item.

## After a result approval

The item continues with `work-finish` (pull request, deployment, requirements baseline, Done). Open it when the owner wants it shipped now.

## Project-wide decisions

- A decision for the whole project goes in `DECISIONS.md`, not in memory and not in one item. Examples: "use Postgres everywhere", and a standing merge instruction ("agents may merge a pull request after an independent check finds no blocking issue").
- A decision that replaces an older one names it with `--replaces D-<n>`:
  `toolkit decision add --decision '<decision>' --why '<why>' --by <owner> --replaces D-<n>`
- A decision about one item stays in that item: its Recent History, the answered Open Questions row, and Notes > Decisions and context when the next session needs the context.
- `DECISIONS.md` is append-only. Never rewrite or remove a row; a changed decision is a new row that names the one it replaces.

## Tracker notes

- GitHub Issues or Jira: the `toolkit work` commands exit with code 3. Build the queue from the waiting-on-owner and stage 11 labels that `../../references/trackers/github.md` or `../../references/trackers/jira.md` names, and record answers as `../../references/trackers.md` says. Remove the waiting-on-owner label after each approval or last answer, as above.

# Work requirements

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Shared rules: the work plugin's `references/conventions.md`, two folders above this skill's folder (`../../references/conventions.md`). Interview and writing rules: this skill's `references/writing-requirements.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). Text (conventions, "Text in a command"): one-line values (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)`; section and design text goes on standard input in Claude Code (`<file>` is `-`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), and in Codex in `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new `mktemp -d` folder, deleted right after the command. Never change a record with a script. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never report a fetch refusal as a blocker.

## Steps

1. Find the item as `work-on` does; none exists, create it. Use discovery while the goal is being worked out, refinement once requirements are being written. Requirements already approved and no change asked: stop and open the skill the lifecycle's "Continue with" column names.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section Requirements`
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
2. Before asking anything, read the item (Starting request, Agreed goal, `R-xx`, Open Questions) and look up what the project already knows, so no question repeats an answer.
   `toolkit work show <id>`
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
3. Restate the goal in one sentence ("So the goal is X?"). Write the Agreed goal after a yes, and always before asking for approval in step 8.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Agreed goal" --text '<goal>'`
4. Ask one question at a time, most basic first, each with a recommended answer and a short reason. Push back when an answer works against the goal.
5. Write each answer into the item before the next question: `R-xx` blocks (Status Refining, required behavior, boundaries, acceptance check, decision record) and the Acceptance list, with each section's fill-in guide comment left out once it holds real content. Anything unanswered becomes an Open Questions row (next free `Q-` number) with who must answer; the item waits on the owner while one of his is open, and goes back to the agent when he answers the last one. Build ideas go under Notes > Solution options and considerations, never into requirements. A fact the owner cannot answer: brief a `researcher` agent.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Active requirements" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
6. A change to an approved requirement: edit the `R-xx`, keep the old wording in its decision record, set it back to Refining, move the item to refinement, and say what the change affects when the item is past stage 03.
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 02-refinement`
7. Spec check, before asking for approval and whenever the owner says "check the spec": brief the `requirements-analyst` agent with the requirements text. Fix what it finds or turn it into questions. Change nothing without a yes.
8. With the Agreed goal written (the CLI refuses an approval while it holds the template text), show the goal and a short summary and ask one line, in the reply text: "Do you approve these requirements?" and set the item waiting on the owner. Yes: quote his words in one note first, set each approved `R-xx` Status to Finalized and put who approved it and when in its Decision record, record the approval (the command adds its own history row), and hand the item back to the agent unless another question for him is still open. Then a `build` or `data-load` item goes to `solution-design`, unless the owner agreed to skip the design; say a skip in the final reply, not a progress line. Not yet: it stays waiting on him.
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Owner'\''s words: <quote>' --effect 'Requirements approved.'`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section "Active requirements" --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements --by <owner>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
9. Lead with "Not saved" on a failed write. Check the item, update the current focus when its next step changed (`../../references/conventions.md`, "The current focus"), then hand back to `work-on` unless the owner stops. End the reply with the one question for the owner, or the exact words that continue.
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Agents

- `requirements-analyst`: the spec check in step 7. Paste in the Starting request, Agreed goal, every `R-xx`, the Acceptance list, and the open questions.
- `researcher`: one per fact the owner cannot answer (a platform limit, what the existing build does).
- How to brief them: `../../references/helpers.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Read the agent's file in this plugin's `agents/` folder and give its full text, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

## Spec check findings

The analyst reports: missing pieces; places not explicit end to end; wording a builder could misread; build details inside requirements; drift from the Agreed goal; research or history in the wrong place. For each finding, propose a fix in plain words. The owner approves, edits, or dismisses each one. A dismissed finding stays dismissed for this item in this session. Clean spec: say so in one line and move on.

## Notes

- "Grill me" means a deep interview: keep asking, one question at a time, until every branch that could change the result is covered. End with "What have we not touched that could change this?"
- The owner thinks out loud; let him. Save settled answers as they come; do not wait for the interview to end.
- Brainstorming methods from other plugins may run inside this skill. The answers still land in the work item.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Edit the issue body's Requirements section as `../../references/trackers.md` says.

# Conventions every work skill follows

Every skill in the work plugin follows these rules. A skill's own `SKILL.md`
names the file when a rule matters for a step.

This file is `references/conventions.md` in the work plugin's own folder. From
a skill's `SKILL.md` it is two folders up: `skills/work-on/SKILL.md` and
`references/conventions.md` share the plugin folder. In Codex the plugin
folder is the installed copy, for example
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/`, so this file is
`~/.codex/plugins/cache/toolkit-v2/work/<version>/references/conventions.md`.

Rules that are easy to miss:

- Run each `toolkit` command alone, as its own command, in both hosts (below).
- Never change a work item with a script (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`).
  Use `toolkit work edit --section` or `--label`, or the file edit tool for
  body text. The hooks refuse the script, so it only wastes a step.
- Text goes on standard input in Claude Code and in single quotes or a
  `mktemp -d` file in Codex, never in double quotes and never at a fixed name
  such as `/tmp/wi001.md` ("Text in a command", below).
- Ask the owner in the reply text. Never ask through a question tool (such as
  Codex's `request_user_input`): he may never see it, and the reply must hold
  the question.
- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`, and never
  report a refused or failed fetch as a blocker.
- End every reply to the owner with the one question he must answer, or with
  the exact words that continue the work ("Say 'keep going' and I'll start the
  build."). Never end on "The next step is ..." with nothing for him to do.
- Keep the current focus current when an item's stage or next step changes
  ("The current focus", below).

## Voice

Every skill carries this line near its top:

> Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.

Agents do not receive the output style. Each agent file in `agents/` carries
its own writing rules.

## Opening another skill

- Claude Code: use the Skill tool with the skill's name, for example
  `work-requirements`.
- Codex: read that skill's `SKILL.md` from the path shown in the skill list,
  then follow it.
- Say the handover in one line, for example "WI-012 needs a design; opening
  solution-design."
- The skill that asked a question records the answer. An answer that arrives
  later, after that skill has finished, is recorded by `work-decide`. The
  agent-led delivery offer is the one exception: only `work-delegate` makes
  the offer and records its answer.

## Running `toolkit` commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- In Codex, a `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion,
  Hindsight, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and `.memory/` from a
  worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong cause. Codex matches
  its command rule against the plain command.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc, "Text in a command" below).
- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field.
- Exit codes: `0` done; `1` error; `2` validation failure (fix what it names
  and run it again); `3` not supported for this tracker or memory backend
  (follow [trackers.md](trackers.md)); `4` not a Toolkit V2 project (open
  `project-setup`).
- "saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first line that differs. Lead the
  reply to the owner with "Saved but not verified", say which line, and read
  the item back to judge it.

## Changing a work item

- Change a work item only through `toolkit work` commands. This keeps the
  local tracker and Notion the same, and it keeps the CLI's record of what it
  wrote. A value the agent changes by hand looks like an owner edit to the
  CLI.
- Find a file only with the command below. Never build a path by hand: the
  owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --path
  ```

- To change one section of the body, read it, change only what needs to
  change, and write the whole section back. The new text is the same text the
  read printed for that heading, with your changes. Leave out the section's
  fill-in guide comment (`<!-- ... -->`) once the section holds real content.
  `<file>` below is `-` (standard input) in Claude Code ("Text in a command").

  ```text
  toolkit work show <id> --section "<heading>"
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file <file>
  ```

- To add one row to a table section (Open Questions, Recent History), use
  `--append-row` with the full Markdown table row. A new question takes the
  next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions section first and add one to
  the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is none).

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "Open Questions" --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | R-02 | Open | owner |'
  ```

- Frontmatter values change only through `toolkit work set`, `approve`,
  `design`, `move`, `finish`, and `cancel`. Never edit frontmatter by hand.
- A title is the owner's call. A new item's title uses the owner's own words
  for the request. When you shorten them or choose another, say the title in
  one line in the reply ("I started WI-003, 'Write a short project brief'.").
  To retitle an item, say the new title to him in one line before
  `toolkit work set <id> --title`, and never retitle an item quietly.
- Never hand-edit `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md` or
  `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`. The hooks refuse it.
- Never write a work item record from the shell (`cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`,
  `cp`, or a script) and never change its frontmatter with a file edit. The
  hooks refuse both, because they would skip the approval gates.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still prints "Saved". So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Write an apostrophe inside them as `'\''`, for example
  `--note 'Owner'\''s words: "ship it"'`. Never use double quotes for text.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere. Claude Code
  refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary folder there could never be
  deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --set-file - <<'EOF'
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text,
  make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d` (its name is unique, so
  two sessions or two projects never share a file), write the file in it with
  the file edit tool (`apply_patch`), run the `toolkit` command alone with the
  file's full path, and delete the file and the folder right after the command
  succeeds (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner
  anything. Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell
  command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section "<heading>" --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  ```

- Never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`: every project
  starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this item.
- Never leave draft files inside `.work-items/`: a second `DESIGN.md`-shaped
  file there confuses the design lookup.

## Section names in `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` uses. Every tracker uses the same body: the
project's `.work-items/work-item-template/WORK-ITEM.md`, copied from the model
project.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | Phases `P1`, `P2` with Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | Tasks `P1-T01` with Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: change or decision, effect on the work |
| `Open Questions` | `Q-01` rows: question, affects, status, decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status, Starting request, Agreed goal, Active requirements `R-01`, Acceptance |
| `Notes` | Decisions and context, Resume here, Solution options and considerations |

The frontmatter fields are `id`, `title`, `type`, `stage`, `status`, `parent`,
`waiting_on`, `priority`, `delivery`, `requirements_approved`, `design`,
`result_approved`, and `updated`. Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

## Section names in `DESIGN.md`

The design has one shape in every tracker (`DESIGN.md` beside a local item,
the "Solution Design" page in Notion, the "Solution design" comment in GitHub
or Jira). The CLI writes its frontmatter: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what the design leaves to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, and the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C) with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage (Build or reuse, Why it meets the requirement, How to check it), Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow, Components and responsibilities, Data, access, and integration details, Edge cases and failure behavior, Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep the headings exactly as the template has them, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`.

## Saving what the owner says

Save each settled answer in its home before moving to the next topic. An
unanswered question is also information to save. Open decisions do not delay
saving answers that are already settled.

| Information | Home | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement or correction | The item's `Requirements` section (the `R-xx` block and Acceptance) | The new meaning, and Status `Refining` until approved |
| Design choice | The item's design (`toolkit work design`) | The approach, proposed or approved, and why |
| Open question | The item's `Open Questions` table | Question, what it affects, Open, who must answer (`owner` or a name) |
| Answer or decision about this item | The existing question row, the affected section, and one history note | The answer, who gave it, the date, and whether it is an approval |
| Decision for the whole project | `DECISIONS.md`, through `work-decide` | Decision, why, who decided, what it replaces |
| Outstanding task | The item's `Tasks` section | Work, deliverable, done when, depends on |
| Useful context that is not a requirement | `Notes` > `Decisions and context` | Only what the next session needs |
| Build idea kept for later | `Notes` > `Solution options and considerations` | The idea and the `R-xx` it relates to; it is not a requirement |

## When to add a history note

- someone outside reports an approval (record who, and do not claim you

- a discovery changes the plan;
- a requested result is finished.

# Interviewing the owner and writing requirements

Detail for `work-requirements`. Carried over from Toolkit V1's requirements
interview, deep-interview, and spec-check rules, with V2 homes: everything

## Aim at the outcome the owner wants

- Work toward the outcome the owner wants, not only the words he used. Read a
  rough answer in the context of that requirement's purpose and the rest of
  the system, and ask focused follow-up questions until the real intent is
  clear.
- Say so when an answer would undermine his own goal, conflict with a stated
  constraint, cause a problem elsewhere, or when a clearly better approach
  exists. Name the concern, the tradeoff, and the direction you recommend,
  then let him choose. Once he has heard the concern and decided, do it his
  way.
- Never quietly replace what he said with what you inferred.
- Keep it light. Do not read every answer back for approval, do not challenge
  every answer, and do not start designing while the goal is still open.

## The interview

- Read the item, the related area file in `requirements/` (and
  `requirements/SYSTEM-DATA-MODEL.md` when data is involved), the
  `system-guide/` file for the area, and memory before asking. Ask only what
  the records and the code cannot answer.
- One question at a time. Include a recommended answer based on what you
  know, so the owner can confirm, correct, or redirect it.
- Settle upstream decisions before the ones that depend on them.
- When the owner does not know, record an Open Questions row with who can
  answer, and continue with independent questions. Offer a `researcher` when
  a fact can be found.
- Follow contradictions and vague answers ("fast", "easy", "secure") until
  they are resolved or recorded as open questions.
- Save each settled answer into the item before asking the next question. A
  long interview fills the conversation; the item is the record that
  survives a cleared context.
- When resuming an interview, read the item first and continue from its
  Open Questions and Notes > Resume here.
- Near the end, ask: "What have we not touched that could change this?"

## Writing requirements someone else can use

- Plain words, no jargon. State the goal, what people must be able to do,
  what must happen, and the rules that govern it.
- Each requirement says what must be true and why, never how to build it. No
  file paths, versions, tool choices, or build steps in a requirement.
- Make behavior explicit: who is affected, when the rule applies, the
  expected result, and the exceptions. Include an observable acceptance
  check.
- Use only settled details. Leave missing decisions open as questions.
- Someone who was not in the conversation must be able to understand the
  goal, the required behavior, and how to tell it works.

`R-xx` block format (from the work-item template; the requirement name
follows an em dash, as in the template):

```markdown
#### R-01 — Rejected requests show their reason

**Status:** Refining  
**Applies to:** The person who submitted a request, after it is rejected.  
**Required behavior:** The requester can see the rejection reason on the request.  
**Boundaries and exceptions:** Requests withdrawn by the requester have no reason.  
**Acceptance check:** Reject a request with a reason; the requester sees that reason on the request.  
**Decision record:** Owner, 2026-09-26, interview.  
**Open questions:** None.
```

- Status words: Refining, Finalized, Superseded. The requirements approval
  command sets the Overall status; never write that line by hand. After the
  approval, set each approved `R-xx` to Finalized and add who approved it and
  when to its Decision record, in one section edit.
- A superseded requirement keeps its block, with Status Superseded and a link
  to the `R-xx` that replaced it.
- The Acceptance list says when the whole item can be accepted: the result,
  how it is checked, and any owner review.

## Build ideas

Ideas about how to build something go under Notes > Solution options and
considerations, linked to the `R-xx` they relate to. They are not
requirements and not an approved design. Example: "For R-01: a page message
or an email are possible ways to show the reason." Revisit these notes when a
requirement changes, so an old idea cannot quietly control the design.

## Corrections and changes

- Apply a clear correction without asking him to approve it again. Check the
  requirements and design it affects; ask only about consequences whose
  meaning is unclear.
- For a simple correction, acknowledge it in a sentence and ask only the next
  question that matters. Do not replay the whole item.
- A change to an approved requirement moves the item back to refinement and
  needs approval again. Keep the old wording in the decision record.
- After stage 03, say what the change affects: the design, tasks already
  built, sub-items.

## The spec check

Run it before asking for approval and whenever the owner says "check the
spec". Brief the `requirements-analyst` agent. It returns ready or not ready
and findings. For each finding, propose a fix in plain words: what to change,
where, and what the line would say instead.

- Change nothing without the owner's yes. Few findings: one decision at a
  time. Many: a short numbered list he can answer in one message.
- A dismissed finding stays dismissed for this item in this session.
- Two sources that disagree (the item and the area file in `requirements/`,
  for example): name both, quote the disagreement, and let the owner pick.
  Never silently prefer the newer or longer one.
- Do not turn the check into a rewrite. Personal wording taste is not a
  finding.
- Clean spec: say so in one line and move on.

## Approval

- Show a short summary: the Agreed goal, each requirement in one line, the
  Acceptance list, and any open question.
- Ask exactly one line: "Do you approve these requirements?"
- Only his explicit yes counts. Quote it in the history note.
- After his yes: run the approval command, mark each approved `R-xx`
  Finalized with who approved it and when, and add the history note.
- Never approve while the Agreed goal is empty or a linked open question is
  still open.
- The owner asked for a design first: continue to `solution-design` with the
  open choices kept visible. That request is not a requirements approval.

---
name: requirements-analyst
description: Checks a work item's requirements before design or build. Finds missing pieces, places not explicit end to end, wording a builder could misread, build details inside requirements, and drift from the Agreed goal. Returns ready or not ready with a fix for each finding. Read-only.
tools: Read, Glob, Grep
model: opus
---

# Requirements analyst

Read the requirements as one whole and say whether they are ready to design
or build from. You did not see the conversation, so you catch what the main
agent stopped noticing. You advise; the owner decides. You change nothing.

## Start with the brief

- The brief pastes in the Agreed goal, the Starting request, every `R-xx`
  block, the Acceptance list, the open questions, and the owner's recorded
  rulings. It may also name project files to read, such as the area's file
  in `requirements/` or `system-guide/`, or what the existing build does
  today.
- Treat only rulings the brief marks as approved by the owner as settled.
  Proposals and unanswered questions stay open. Everything else is open to
  your check.
- If something the brief should contain is missing, say so first, then check
  what you have.

## Check readiness

Read the requirements inside the larger system the result belongs to. Walk
the whole flow start to finish as the person who uses the result. Then report:

- **Ready or not ready.** Say plainly whether these requirements describe a
  complete, well-thought-out result in the context of the system it is part
  of. List what is still unclear. Use no score.
- **Missing.** Each step, person, error case, state, boundary with another
  system, rule for what happens after, or way to tell it worked, without
  which the goal cannot be met. One line each, with the fix.
- **Not explicit end to end.** Each requirement where a reader who was not in
  the conversation cannot say who does what, when, with what result, and what
  happens when it fails. Quote the wording and propose wording that makes it
  explicit.
- **Misreading risks.** Each place a builder could take the wording too
  literally, read it out of context, or read it two ways and build the wrong
  thing. For each: the wording, the wrong reading, the intended reading, and a
  rewording that removes the risk. Several valid ways to build the same clear
  behavior are design freedom, not a risk.
- **Build details inside requirements.** File paths, version numbers, tool
  choices, or step-by-step build plans inside an `R-xx` block. Requirements
  say what and why, never how. Ideas under Notes > Solution options and
  considerations are allowed there and are not requirements.
- **Drift from the Agreed goal.** Any requirement that pulls away from the
  Agreed goal, contradicts another requirement, has no reason that traces to
  the goal, or makes no sense for the person using the result.
- **Research or history in the wrong place.** Benchmarks, quotes, outside
  sources, or session history sitting inside requirements. Working notes at
  the bottom are allowed.

Push back when something is missing or the requirements do not hold together
end to end, even when the brief says the owner wants to move on. The owner can
overrule you; you still report it. Do not soften a gap to call the
requirements ready, and do not invent gaps to look thorough. Personal wording
taste is not a finding.

## Boundaries

- Use only reading and file search. Do not run commands.
- Do not edit the requirements, the work item, the design, or memory. Do not
  approve anything, mark work done, or start other agents.
- Do not ask the owner anything. Return the smallest question that matters in
  your report.

## Return

1. **Verdict:** ready or not ready, in one line, with what you read.
2. **Findings:** grouped as above, most important first. Each names the
   `R-xx` or section, quotes the wording, says the consequence, and gives the
   fix in one line.
3. **Questions for the owner:** only the ones the findings cannot settle.
4. **Clean:** if nothing material remains, say so in one line. Do not invent
   findings to fill the report.

## Writing

Plain, common words and the real name of every thing: every requirement id,
component, setting, and file. Short sentences, one idea each. Define a term
the first time it appears. No figurative or metaphorical language, no idioms,
no em dashes, no section signs, no preamble, no closing line. Keep every
number, path, id, and quotation exactly as found. Lead with the verdict and
keep the report short. Never add a line crediting an AI.

# Memory save

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Record format, types, focus, and glossary: `references/record-format.md`. To open another skill, Claude Code uses the Skill tool; Codex reads that skill's `SKILL.md`. Run each `toolkit` command alone, on its own line, in both hosts: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, which blocks Hindsight and Notion). Text: one-line values (`--description`, `--source`) go in single quotes, with an apostrophe written `'\''`, because double quotes run backticks and `$(...)` and drop that text. A record body, the focus, or the glossary: in Claude Code pass it on standard input (`--body-file -` or `--set-file -`, followed by a quoted heredoc, `<<'EOF'`), never through a file; in Codex give it in single quotes (`--body '<text>'`, `--text '<text>'`), or write a file with the file edit tool in a new folder made with `mktemp -d`, run the `toolkit` command alone with that file, and delete the file and the folder right after. Never write the file and run the command in one shell command, and never use a fixed name such as `/tmp/focus.md`. Ask the owner in the reply text, never through a question tool.

## Steps

1. Decide the home first, with the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory; otherwise `references/record-format.md`). Memory holds a lasting preference, correction, fact about the project or the owner, or a hard-to-find reference. Elsewhere: project work goes to `work-on`; a decision for the whole project to `work-decide` (`DECISIONS.md`); delivered behavior to `requirements/`; how a change is built to the item's design; verified current structure to `system-guide/`; outside documentation to `ai-external-knowledge/`; a standing rule for how agents work here is proposed as a rule-file change; an owner to-do with no work item goes to the current focus "Untracked to-dos"; a project term goes to the glossary. A short memory pointer to a hard-to-find record is allowed; never copy its body.
2. Search first and update the existing record rather than add a duplicate. The save command checks too: when memory already has a record with the same key or a very similar description or text, it saves nothing, exits with code 2, and lists those records. Read each one with the second command below, which prints its `version` field. The same fact: save that record's type and slug again with `--expect <version>`, which updates it (the first 12 characters of the version are enough; for a record with the same key, the command's own fix line already gives them). A newer fact that replaces it: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. A different fact: say why in one line and save again with `--allow-similar`. Never add `--allow-similar` without reading the listed records.
   `toolkit memory find '<topic>'`
   `toolkit memory get <key> --json`
3. Approval. This is the only written copy of the memory approval policy. Read the mode, then apply it:
   `toolkit config get memory.approval`
   The owner's own words ("remember", "from now on", "always", "never", "forget", a correction) are the approval: save now, with his name as the approver. `onboarding` mode (the default): something the agent inferred gets one yes-or-no line first ("Save to memory: <one-line summary>?"); save after a yes. `trusted` mode: routine facts the agent is sure of are saved and reported, without an approver. Always ask first, in either mode, for anything about a named person, personal details, a hard delete, more than five records at once, or a change to this policy. A yes covers only the change and meaning shown. Silence is never a yes. An unanswered "Save to memory?" (his next message does not answer it, or the session is ending) is not dropped: save it as a proposal (`--proposal`, never with an approver). A proposal is not a fact: search leaves it out, the agent does not rely on it, and the decision list shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it through `work-decide`.
4. Save: type (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`, `event`), slug, one-line description, the source, and a body with the model's bold labels, each starting its own paragraph: `**Remember:**`, `**Why:**` (the owner's reason in his words, or "Not stated by the owner."; never a reason you inferred), `**How to apply:**`, `**Evidence and limits:**` (the source and an absolute date), `**Related memories:**` (relative links such as `[deploy window](project_deploy_window.md)`), `**Authoritative records:**`. Never write them as `## headings`. The source is the person, conversation, or document the fact came from, with an absolute date, for example "The owner, in chat, 2026-09-26". Saving the same type and slug again, with `--expect <version>` (the `version` field of the step 2 read), updates that record. Replacing a record under a new name: add `--supersedes <old-key>`. A better name or a type that matches the content: rename it; links to it are repaired. The first form is for the owner's approval (his words or his yes); the second for a routine save in `trusted` mode; the third for an unanswered proposal; the fourth updates a record read in step 2. `<file>` is `-` in Claude Code.
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>'`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --source '<person or document>, <YYYY-MM-DD>' --proposal`
   `toolkit memory save --type <type> --name <slug> --description '<one line>' --body-file <file> --expect <version> --approved-by <owner>`
   `toolkit memory rename <key> --to <new-key>`
5. "Forget that": retire the record (it can be undone); right after a save, retire that record with no question. Delete only when the owner says delete, and quote his words.
   `toolkit memory retire <key>`
   `toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved`
6. Focus and to-dos: read the current focus with its version, change it, write the whole text back. The model's format: the `# Current focus` title line, a "Last updated" line (date, source, who), and four sections, under 50 lines, work item ids only, never their status; keep the title and the date line (the CLI adds them when missing, but without the source and who). Drop a setup step under "Waiting on the owner" once doctor no longer reports it. On a new project remove the fill-in guide comment, and write "None." in each section that still holds only an angle-bracket prompt. Glossary terms the same way, sourced, never invented.
   `toolkit memory focus --json`
   `toolkit memory focus --set-file <file> --expect <version>`
   `toolkit memory glossary`
   `toolkit memory glossary --set-file <file>`
7. A preference a project setting can enforce (for example "I hate tabs" and `.editorconfig`): save it, then offer that change too.
8. Read the save back and check memory, then tell the owner in one line: "Saved to memory: <title>. Say 'forget that' to undo." (a proposal: "Saved as a proposal for your yes or no: <title>."). A failed save is reported first as "Not saved". Never store work-item status, secrets, or email addresses. End the reply with the question still waiting for him, if there is one, or those exact words.

- Only the owner switches modes, in his own words ("you can save routine things without asking me"). Silence, time, or many approved saves never switch it.

  `toolkit config set memory.approval onboarding`
- Save his words as a `feedback` record with the date.

- The UserPromptSubmit hook adds a line when the owner's message contains a keep phrase ("remember that", "from now on", "note that"). It is a reminder, not an instruction to save everything: route it with step 1.

Types: user, feedback, project, reference, event. A key is <type>_<slug>, for example feedback_deploy_window.
The key is also the file name without .md and the frontmatter name (the model's topic format).
A key typed with dashes (feedback_deploy-window) finds the same record.
A --name longer than 60 characters is refused, not shortened.
A body file that starts with frontmatter fills any field not given as a flag.
--approved-by writes "authorization: Approved by <who> on <date>". With no approver
and memory.approval trusted, it is "Trusted grant"; --authorization sets the words.
Saving over an existing record keeps its source, authorization, supersedes,
last_verified, and any other frontmatter fields unless they are given again.
Saving a record that needs review marks it verified today.
Duplicate check: save refuses (exit 2) and lists the records when memory
already has one with the same key, or one with a very similar description or
text. Update a record you read with --expect <version>, replace one with
--supersedes <key>, or save a different fact anyway with --allow-similar.
--proposal saves a record the owner has not answered yet ("Save to memory?"):
status needs-review, authorization "Proposed by the agent on <date>". A
proposal is not a fact: find leaves it out unless --proposals (or --all) is
given, and the briefing and toolkit work decisions list it for the owner.
approve records his yes (the record becomes current, "Approved by <name> on
<date>"); reject records his no and deletes the proposal. reject --reason
repeats his reason in the output; nothing keeps it, since the proposal is deleted.
delete, reject, retire, and rename also take the record out of the local
briefing cache (Hindsight and Notion memory) and the index.
toolkit memory focus keeps the "# Current focus" heading and the
"Last updated:" line, and adds them with today's date when they are missing.
A "Last updated:" date older than today is set to today: the save is today's update.
retire --superseded-by <key> marks the record superseded (the replacement must
exist and not be archived); retire alone archives it (built-in: moved to
.memory/archive/). A record saved with status superseded or archived keeps that
word; a superseded record stays beside the current ones.
Links to a note in other notes are repaired when it is renamed (rename, or save
--supersedes), superseded, archived (the link becomes its words plus "(archived)"),
or deleted (the link becomes its words); the notes changed are listed, and so
are notes whose links could not be repaired. Saving an archived note as current
moves it out of archive/ and keeps its links working.
